title: What If Shadows Weighed 50 Kilograms?
sources: NOAA / National Weather Service, Sun angle and shadows: at local solar noon the sun is at its highest elevation, so a shadow is at its shortest and sits directly beneath the object
NOAA / National Weather Service: as the sun sinks toward the horizon in the afternoon the same object casts a much longer shadow, because the light rays arrive at a shallow angle
NASA Science, light travels in straight lines: an opaque object blocks those rays and the blocked region on the ground is the shadow

lines.text: Just step outside at noon and fifty kilograms locks right onto your ankles.
lines.caps: Just *step | outside at *noon | fifty *kilograms | locks onto your *ankles.

lines.text: At high noon, the sun hangs almost straight above your head.
lines.caps: At *high noon | the *sun hangs | almost straight *above | your *head.

lines.text: That leaves your shadow as a small dark puddle under your shoes.
lines.caps: That leaves your *shadow | a small dark *puddle | under your *shoes.

lines.text: By four o'clock the sun drops low, and stretches your shadow ten feet behind you.
lines.caps: By *four o'clock | the sun *drops low | and *stretches | ten feet *behind you.

lines.text: Then that weight yanks you flat onto the sidewalk.
lines.caps: Then that *weight | yanks you *flat | onto the *sidewalk.

lines.text: Slip under an umbrella or into a dark room, and the weight drops to zero.
lines.caps: Slip under an *umbrella | into a dark *room, | the weight *drops | to *zero.

lines.text: But the second a cloud drifts over, all fifty kilograms slam back onto your heels.
lines.caps: But the *second | a cloud *drifts over | all fifty *kilograms | slam back *onto | your *heels.
